title: Starting hands and the 13×13 grid
summary: Combos, range notation and what makes a hand strong.

combos.text:
A deck gives **1326** different two-card hands: **combos**. Suits don't matter before the flop, so they are grouped into **169 hand classes**:
- **Pairs** (AA, 77): 6 combos each.
- **Suited** hands (AKs): 4 combos.
- **Offsuit** hands (AKo): 12 combos.
- Plain "AK" means AKs and AKo together, 16 combos.

grid.text:
All 169 classes fit into a **13×13 grid**: pairs on the diagonal, suited hands above it, offsuit hands below. Ranges are written in short **notation**:
- **77+**: sevens and every higher pair.
- **ATs+**: ATs, AJs, AQs, AKs.
- **KJo+**: KJo and KQo.
- **A5s-A2s**: from A5s down to A2s.
- **98o:0.5**: 98o half of the time.

notation.caption: The range "77+, ATs+, KJo+" on the grid.

strength.text:
What makes a starting hand strong:
- **High cards and pairs** make top pair or a set more often.
- **Suitedness** adds about 3% equity from flushes.
- **Connectedness**: 87s makes straights far more often than 82s.
- **Domination**: AQ against AK usually loses on the kicker and has only about 26%.

labels: AK vs 77: 44%, close to a coin flip
equities.caption: Preflop equity with both hands face up and the whole board dealt.

q-combos.q: How many combos of AKo are there?
q-combos.explain: 4 aces times 4 kings is 16 combinations. 4 of them are suited, so 12 are offsuit.

t1.q: How many combos does any pocket pair, such as 88, have?
t1.explain: Two of four eights can be chosen in 4×3/2 = 6 ways.

t2.explain: "+" on a suited hand moves the lower card up to just below the higher one: KTs, KJs, KQs.

t3.q: Why does AQ do badly against AK?
options: It's dominated: when an ace comes it loses on the kicker
t3.explain: When both pair the ace the kicker decides, and the king beats the queen. That's why AQ has only about 26% against AK.
